en: Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty, this is the *Gopālaka Sūtra* as spoken by the Buddha.
In the garden,
at that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are eleven things regarding which a cowherd boy does not know the proper way to tend cattle, nor is he skilled in raising them.”

What are these eleven? First, the cowherd boy does not know colors; second, he does not know marks; third, he does not know how to groom them; fourth, he does not know how to protect wounds; fifth, he does not know how to produce smoke; sixth, he does not know how to choose the path for travel; seventh, he does not know how to care for the cattle; eighth, he does not know which path to take when crossing water; ninth, he does not know how to pursue good grass and water; tenth, he milks the cows until nothing remains; and eleventh, he does not know how to distinguish between those that can be raised and those that cannot.
"Bhikṣus! If a cowherd boy does not understand how to care for and protect these eleven matters, his cattle will never multiply; rather, they will diminish day by day."

One who does not know how to practice these eleven matters, like a cowherd’s child, will never become a true śramaṇa; within this Dharma, they will never plant the roots of the Vinaya, and thus there will be no leaves, branches, or shade.
Those who do not practice these eleven matters yet forcibly claim to be śramaṇas will fall into the three evil realms after death.
What are the eleven practices of a bhikṣu? A bhikṣu does not know form; he does not know its characteristics;

when it is time to scrub, he does not know how to scrub; when it is time to protect a wound, he does not know how to protect it; when it is time to produce smoke, he does not know how to produce it; he does not know how to choose the path for walking; he does not know how to tend the cow; he does not know which way to cross the water; he does not know the proper place for eating; and he does not know how to respect his elders.
“Monks! How is it that one does not know form? Monks!”
“Monks, one does not know the four great elements, nor does one know the form derived from the four great elements;
in this way, monks, one does not know.”
What is the characteristic of not knowing? Bhikṣus!
It is not knowing the characteristic of the causal conditions for delusion, and not knowing the characteristic of the causal conditions for wisdom.
What is the characteristic of ignorance regarding the conditions for delusion? Bhikṣus!
One does not know the conditions for the dark, one does not know the conditions for the bright, and one does not know the conditions for the dark-and-bright.
What is meant by not knowing the mark of wisdom?
It is not knowing the dark conditions, not knowing the bright conditions, and not knowing the conditions that are both dark and bright. Monks!
In this way, monks, they do not understand the characteristic [of the mind].
How is it that one should scrub and polish, yet does not scrub and polish?

"Monks! If a mind of desire arises and one takes pleasure in it, becoming attached to it, not relinquishing it, not forgetting it, and not severing it, then delusion, greed, stinginess, and other evil states of mind will arise; one harbors them all within and does not vomit them out or abandon them."
In this way, bhikṣus,
one should polish and scrub, yet you have not polished and scrubbed. Bhikṣus!
What is meant by "one who should protect the wound but does not protect the wound"? Bhikṣus!

Upon seeing forms, one gives rise to perceptions; upon hearing sounds, one becomes attached. One contemplates physical appearances and does not recognize them as evil. Failing to guard the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, one rushes toward external objects and is unable to restrain oneself.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
You should protect a wound, yet you do not protect the wound. How so, bhikṣus?
"Should one produce smoke but fail to produce it?
Bhikṣu! One has studied and heard [the teachings], yet does not know how to explain them to others."
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should produce smoke, yet you do not produce smoke. How so, bhikṣus?"
"Do you not know how to choose the path to practice? Bhikṣu!
You do not enter the direct path to practice, but instead travel upon a non-path."
What is practicing a non-path? Bhikṣu!
Entering the quarters of courtesans, as well as places of drinking, gambling, and games.
In this way, bhikṣus,
one does not know the path of practice.
How is it that a bhikṣu does not know craving?
"Monks! When the jewel of the Dharma is being taught, they do not listen with a sincere heart of love and joy.
It is thus, monks!"
This is due to ignorance regarding craving.
How so, bhikṣu? What is meant by not knowing how to cross over the water?
"Monks! You do not know the Four Noble Truths.
What are the Four Noble Truths?"
"Monks! One does not know the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
It is thus, monks!"
It is because they do not know how to cross over the waters. How is it, bhikṣu,
that they do not know the proper place for food?
"Monks! You do not know the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four foundations of mindfulness?"

"Monks! One does not know how to contemplate the body internally, contemplate the body externally, or contemplate the body both internally and externally; one does not know how to contemplate feelings internally, contemplate feelings externally, or contemplate feelings both internally and externally; one does not know how to contemplate the mind internally, contemplate the mind externally, or contemplate the mind both internally and externally; one does not know how to contemplate phenomena internally, contemplate phenomena externally, or contemplate phenomena both internally and externally."
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
This is not knowing the proper place for food. How so, bhikṣus?
"Do you not know that the food will not suffice? Bhikṣu!

Suppose you have been invited by a king, a householder, or a faithful man or woman to a meal, and they have served you various kinds of delicacies with sincere devotion. If you, bhikṣu, do not know moderation, and after eating there is still a remainder, you wish to take it back home."
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
It is because one does not know how to eat without leaving a remainder. How so, bhikṣus?
"Do you not know how to revere the elders? Bhikṣus!
What is meant by 'not knowing how to revere and make offerings'?"

Suppose there is an elder bhikṣu who has long practiced the Way and its virtue, whose learning is vast and profound; yet a junior bhikṣu does not pay him homage with a sincere heart, fails to rise upon seeing him, does not vacate his seat for him, treats him with contempt and mockery, and does not attend to him with a virtuous mind.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!

Not knowing how to respect one's elders, if there is a bhikṣu who does not know how to practice these eleven dharmas, he should not be considered a śramaṇa within my Dharma. He has not planted the roots of the Law; lacking branches, leaves, and protective shade, he will rot away from within. It would be better for him to return to being a white-robed layman.
"If one is forcibly made a śramaṇa, he will surely enter the three evil realms.
Bhikṣu! Know that a cowherd has eleven practices for tending and protecting [his cattle], by which he can cause them to flourish and multiply."
What are the eleven? This cowherd boy knows the colors, knows the marks, brushes [the cows],

protects their sores, raises smoke, chooses the path, crosses waters, loves the cows, follows them to water and grass, knows the proper measure of milk left after milking, distinguishes between good and bad cows, and tends to those that are serviceable.
"In this way, the cowherd is able to nurture, protect, and increase his cattle.
Thereupon the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The cowherd is discerning, The owner of the cattle possesses merit; [The cattle will thrive]."
Six oxen for six years, yielding sixty without decrease.
The cowherd boy was intelligent, knowing how to distinguish their various characteristics.
A cowherd boy such as this was praised by Buddhas of former ages.

“Monks, when these eleven qualities are practiced, one is able to plant the roots of the Dharma and Vinaya within these teachings; its branches and leaves will flourish and provide shade over the great earth, never again to decay.”
What are these eleven?

A bhikṣu knows form, knows characteristics, knows cleansing, knows bandaging wounds, knows when to produce smoke, knows the path of practice, knows affection, knows crossing water, knows the place of eating, knows non-exhaustion, and knows how to respect, honor, and provide for those who are elders, long-studying, and venerable.
How does a bhikṣu know form? Bhikṣu!
He knows that form is produced by the four great elements. Thus it is, bhikṣu!
For the sake of knowing form:
how does a bhikṣu know its characteristics? Bhikṣu!
There is a distinction between delusion and wisdom. What is delusion?
To think what should not be thought, to act what should not be done, and to speak what should not be spoken—this is delusion.
What is wisdom?
To contemplate what is to be contemplated, to practice what is to be practiced, and to speak what is to be spoken—this is wisdom.
To be able to distinguish between delusion and wisdom is the characteristic of knowledge.
How should a bhikṣu cleanse and know how to cleanse? Bhikṣu!

If a thought of desire arises, he is able to restrain it and distance himself from it, as if vomiting out a loathsome view; if anger, stinginess, greed, or any other evils arise, he is able to restrain them and distance himself from them, as if vomiting out a loathsome view.
In this way, bhikṣus, you should know what is to be cleansed by cleansing. How,
bhikṣus, should one guard a wound by guarding it?

"Monks! When the eye sees forms, one does not discriminate between the beautiful and the ugly; one guards the faculty of the eye and does not cling to external forms. One distances oneself from and abandons all evils, protecting the faculty of the eye. When the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue tastes flavors, the body craves smoothness, and the mind harbors many thoughts, one restrains them so they do not lead to attachment. One protects these faculties so as not to be defiled by external objects, just as one rejects and spits out evil views."
In this way, bhikṣus,
one knows how to protect a wound.
How does a bhikṣu emit smoke from time to time?
"Monks! As you have been taught, heard, and known, explain this in detail: in this way, a monk is one who knows when smoke is being emitted.
How does a monk know the path of practice?"

A bhikṣu practices the eightfold path of careful discernment; knowing places that should not be frequented—such as brothels, taverns, and gambling dens—he never enters them recklessly. In this way, a bhikṣu is one who knows the path to be traveled.
How does a bhikṣu know love? Bhikṣu!
When seeing the Dharma-jewel being preached, one listens and receives it with a sincere heart, leaping for joy and cherishing it with love; such a bhikṣu is said to know love.
How does a bhikṣu know the place for crossing the water? Bhikṣu!
He knows the Four Noble Truths.
What are the Four Truths?
They are the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, a bhikṣu is one who knows how to cross the waters.
How does a bhikṣu know the proper place for food? Bhikṣu!
He knows the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four foundations of mindfulness? Monks!

One contemplates the body internally, contemplates the body externally, and contemplates the body both internally and externally; one contemplates feelings internally, contemplates feelings externally, and contemplates feelings both internally and externally; one contemplates the mind internally, contemplates the mind externally, and contemplates the mind both internally and externally; one contemplates phenomena internally, contemplates phenomena externally, and contemplates phenomena both internally and externally. In this way, monks, one is said to know the proper sphere of nutriment.
How does a bhikṣu know moderation regarding food? Bhikṣu!

If kings, householders, laymen, or laywomen, with a heart of faith and joy, invite a bhikṣu and provide him with various kinds of fine foods and delicacies as offerings, and if they treat him with increased respect and encourage him to eat, the bhikṣu, knowing the proper measure for the sake of sustaining the body, shall stop; he reflects upon the words of the Buddha:
"Though the donor's offerings be abundant, one should know one's own limit and not accept them all.
In this way, a bhikṣu knows moderation regarding food.
How does a bhikṣu know how to respect those who are senior, long-practiced, and venerable, honoring and making offerings to them?

"Monks! You should associate with such people, honoring and making offerings to them; when they enter or leave, you should go out to meet them or step aside to yield your seat upon seeing them come; you should serve them to the best of your ability, without indolence or arrogance."
In this way, a bhikṣu knows how to revere his elders. Bhikṣus!
Those who are able to practice these eleven matters plant the roots of the Dharma and Vinaya within this teaching; their branches and leaves flourish, providing abundant shade, pure and stainless.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Those who possess faith and diligence in training, Who know moderation in receiving food,
And who show reverence to their elders— Such conduct is praised by the Buddhas."
"If a bhikṣu trains in these eleven dharmas,
concentrating his mind day and night, he shall attain arhatship within six years.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on Tending Cattle Spoken by the Buddha
